---
name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

432	/// flags that ask nothing of the parsing style, those no constant names included, do not

436	/// [`std::env::var_os`] returning `Some`: libc's `getenv` takes its `std` route. The variable

content.content:
### `git2/src/cli/opt.c` wave 186 batch 0: `opt.h`'s enums

The first batch of the `git2` link unit, the CLI. It ports `src/cli/opt.h`'s four enums into
`src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`, as native Rust that keeps C's values. `enm::cli_opt_type_t` is
`Kind` and `enm::cli_opt_status_t` is `Status`: closed enums, as the plan judges them (their
`port/layout` is wave 2404). Each is `#[repr(u32)]` with C's discriminants, and has
crate-private `from_raw` / `raw` conversions for the gateways the module's later batches
write. Each conversion carries a `dead_code` expectation outside tests until a gateway calls
it (`crustify/evolution/enum-integer-form-crate-private`). `enm::cli_opt_usage_t` is `Usage`
and `enm::cli_opt_flag_t` is `ParseFlags`: `#[repr(transparent)]` bit sets over `u32` that
keep unnamed bits, as the spec tables' `HIDDEN | STOP_PARSING` and `CHOICE | SHOW_LONG` need.
Each of the 23 constants is anchored on its variant or associated constant. The file holds no
unsafe region and carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Nothing is exported: `opt.h` keeps the C
definitions for `cmd_*.c`, `common.c`, `main.c` and `opt_usage.c`. The enums hold no pointer,
so wavefront has no ownership finding or lifecycle to submit for them. `sys/git2/allowlist.txt`
gains the four typedefs, and its bindings were regenerated in campaign mode; they are
constants alone, so nothing new links.

Tests: eight `unit_pub` tests. They cover each flag being its own bit, the spec tables'
combinations under `contains`, `intersects`, `&` and `|`, the assigning operators, unnamed
bits retained, the closed enums' C values in `opt.h`'s order, and the derived traits. Four
`equiv` tests compare every variant's discriminant and every flag's bits with `sys::git2`'s
constants, and four `equiv_priv` tests in `lib` round-trip the conversions through those
constants and refuse values past them. The CLI has no C tests to carry over. The test counts
are by binary, so `lib`'s four are in the unit column. The API stability row counts the
worklist's 27 anchors, the four enums and their 23 constants, all `new`. Of the unattributed
modules, `sys::git2` is `extended` by the raw constants and the other 18 are `kept`.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on a `git archive` of the wave
tip `2216b0cd0` and on this tree, and read with `report.py` (`C=@c` over the `coverage`
variant's `libcrustify.a`, Rust over the scratch tree's `src/`). The unit column merges `lib`
and `unit_pub`. Per `coverage-report-relative-rows`, the base was read from `src/libgit2`, but
the tree from `src/`: `opt.rs` now holds counted regions, so `llvm-cov`'s common prefix is
`src/`. `opt.rs` is covered in full: 81 of 81 lines, 22 of 22 functions and 81 of 81 regions.
A first measurement left `ParseFlags`' binary `&` unrun, and a test was added for it. The C
shifts (`-0.02` pp `equiv`, `-0.05` pp unit) come from suites whose new tests run no C, so
they are run-to-run variation. The Rust shifts are the denominator's 81 new lines. The
Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+158`, the regenerated bindings
included) and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+261`). `+LoC` counts every `.rs` line, `bindings.rs`'s
89 among them. `ported types` counts the four enums against the recorded total.

The safety audit scans (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`, no export feature in the manifest) move only `unsafe loc %`
(`-0.08` pp, from the new safe lines). The boundary scan's sites hold none in the changeset.

Gates, on the base `2216b0cd0`: the workspace is formatted, and `clippy --all-targets` passes
with warnings denied. The module's tests pass on `plain` and under ASan+UBSan, and all 16
pass under Miri: they read constants alone. The coverage runs ran every suite of both trees
(`lib` 844 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 761, `ub_unsafe` 120, `equiv` 532, `unit_pub` 75,
`hidden_symbols` 1, doctests 377 merged). Only the known `CommitBuilder` compile-fail
doctest fails, on both trees. TSan and BSan have no obligation: there is no unsafe code, no
`Send` or `Sync` claim and no thread. The raw bindings changed, so the crate was packaged in
bundled mode (698 files) and verified. That took the unpublished wrappers patched on
`crates-io` and the side campaigns' installs on `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`, colon-separated
(`crustify/evolution/packaging-gate-procedure`). Usage cells are the assistant's.


### `git2/src/cli/opt.c` wave 186 batch 1: `spec_is_option_type` and `support_gnu_style`

The wave's symbol route: the TU-local macro `mac::spec_is_option_type` and the static function
`fn::support_gnu_style`, ported as native Rust into `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`, beside batch 0's
enums. Both use those enums' constants, which wavefront records no use of
(`crustify/evolution/wavefront-enum-constant-uses`, whose evidence this batch extends): the
macro compares a spec's `type` with `CLI_OPT_TYPE_BOOL`, `_SWITCH` and `_VALUE`, and the function
tests `CLI_OPT_PARSE_FORCE_GNU` and `CLI_OPT_PARSE_GNU`. The batch was written against stand-ins
of batch 0's in-progress types and rebased onto its landing, `8a149ac08`, where it takes `Kind`
and `ParseFlags`. `spec_is_option_type` is `Kind::is_option`, a `const fn` over the spec's kind,
which a ported spec's kind answers; the C parser's long-argument branch for an accumulator stays
unreachable, as in the C, and no spec of the CLI is one. `support_gnu_style` is
`uses_gnu_style(ParseFlags) -> bool`: rustdoc refuses an alias equal to its item's name, so the
port is renamed and keeps the alias (`crustify/evolution/doc-alias-equal-to-the-name`). It reads
`POSIXLY_CORRECT` through `std::env::var_os`, libc's `getenv` taking its recommended `std` route,
which held exactly: the C tests presence alone, the empty value included. Nothing is exported:
no C outside `opt.c` reaches either item. The file keeps `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. The
`loc` cell is wavefront's `query dag --loc`, `0` for the macro and `18` for the function.

The `git2` allowlist gains `cli_opt_parser_init` and `cli_opt_parser_next`, which the
equivalence tests reach the C through, and the bindings were regenerated in campaign mode,
833 lines: the two functions, `cli_opt_spec`, `cli_opt` and `cli_opt_parser`, whose bitfields
bring bindgen's `__BindgenBitfieldUnit`. Those helpers and `cli_opt_parser`'s `*_raw`
accessors are the safety audit row's `+10` public `unsafe fn`s, `+30` raw dereferences and `+37`
unsafe blocks, all in the generated `sys/git2/bindings.rs`; the safe crate's own counts do not
move, and the boundary scan's sites hold none in the hand-written changeset.

Tests: six `unit_pub` tests (the kinds a long name selects, the predicate in a `const` block,
`FORCE_GNU`, the default, unnamed flag bits, and `GNU` under `POSIXLY_CORRECT` unset, `1`, empty
and `0`, each in a child process of the test binary, since setting the environment is unsafe
beside the harness's threads), two `equiv` tests and two doctests. The equivalence of the macro
goes through `cli_opt_parser_next`, which parses `--opt` against every non-empty subset of the
seven listed kinds, in order and reversed, every spec named `opt`: the C's selected spec is the
first the Rust's predicate accepts, with the status that follows. That of the function goes
through `cli_opt_parser_init`'s `needs_sort`, for the four combinations of the style flags, each
beside none or three sets of unnamed bits, in three child environments. Mutating either port
(an accumulator as an option; `GNU` ignoring the variable) fails its equivalence test. The CLI
has no C tests to carry over. Worklist coverage: `opt.rs` 90 of 90 lines, 24 of 24 functions,
92 of 92 regions; C `support_gnu_style` every line, each branch reached, and the macro's line
of `spec_for_long` 224 times.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on this tree and read with
`report.py` from the scratch tree's `src/` (`C=@c` over the `coverage` variant's
`libcrustify.a`, `Rust=.`), the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`; the base is batch 0's
measurement of the tip it landed, recorded in `Coverage stats`, not measured again. The shifts
in suites whose new tests run no C (`ub_safe`, `ub_unsafe`) are run-to-run variation; `equiv`'s
`+0.12` pp C is the parser lines its new tests reach. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's
`code.loc.total` (`+695`, the regenerated bindings included) and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+226`).
`+LoC` counts every `.rs` line, `bindings.rs`'s 833 among them. `ported symbols` counts the two
items against the recorded total.

The safety audit scan (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`, no export feature in the manifest) is compared with batch 0's
scan of the tip. `ffimap api` against the tip, with ffibox's private rustdoc JSON (nightly
`2026-10-08`): both items are `new`; of the unattributed modules `sys::git2` is `extended`, the
other 18 `kept`.

Gates, all on the rebased tree (`8a149ac08` plus this batch): the workspace is formatted, and
`clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied. The whole workspace passes on `plain` (`lib`
844 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 762, `ub_unsafe` 120, `equiv` 534, `unit_pub` 81, `hidden_symbols`
1, doctests 74 merged and 378 standalone). The module's tests (`lib` 4, `equiv` 6, `unit_pub`
14, doctests 2) pass under ASan+UBSan, and under Miri all but three, each run alone there and
seen to stop: the two child-process tests at `current_exe` (`spawns a process`) and the macro's
equivalence test at `cli_opt_parser_init` (`calls C`). The coverage runs ran every suite; only
the known `CommitBuilder` compile-fail doctest fails. TSan and BSan have no obligation: the
batch adds no unsafe code to the safe crate, no `Send` or `Sync` claim and no thread. The raw
bindings changed, so the crate was packaged in bundled mode and verified, by batch 0's command
(`crustify/evolution/packaging-gate-procedure`). Usage cells are the assistant's.


### `git2/src/cli/opt.c` wave 186 batch 2: `cli_opt_spec`, `cli_opt` and `cli_opt_parser`

The type route of waves 187 and 188, folded onto wave 186: `st::cli_opt_spec`, `st::cli_opt` and
`st::cli_opt_parser`, wrapped in `ffi_import` of `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs` beside batches 0 and
1's ports, since `main.c`, `common.c`, `opt_usage.c` and the `cmd_*.c` spec tables use their
layouts until `port/layout` (waves 1988 and 2404). `define_ctype!` mints `Spec<'p>`, `Opt<'p>`
and `Parser<'p>` with their `Ref`/`Mut` handles, each invariant in `'p`, the borrow of what it
points at, and none `Send` or `Sync`. Each typedef shares its struct's name, so the struct's
layout carries the `tdf::` anchor too. All three are `CZeroable`: a zeroed spec ends a table, a
zeroed outcome is the one `cli_opt_parser_next` clears, and a zeroed parser has no table. Nothing
is owned, so there is no policy and no owner. `Parser::new` is the `init` constructor,
`fn::cli_opt_parser_init`, which wavefront had no role for: it is now in the ownership store,
with the 13 pointer fields' findings.

A spec's `type` and type-erased `value` form one `Target<'p>`, read from both fields and written
together, since the kind decides the pointee: `&Cell<c_int>` for a bool, switch or accumulator,
`&Cell<Option<Arg>>` for a value or argument, `&ArgsSlot` for the remaining arguments. These are
`Cell`s because switches multiplexing one mode share a variable. `Arg<'p>` is a borrowed C string
as a non-null `char *`, so the parser's arguments are a real `[Arg<'p>]`, exclusively borrowed and
reordered in place through `ParserMut::args_mut`. `ArgsSlot` keeps C's `&args[idx]` as a position
that is never read through; `get_in` finds the tail in the parser's array. `SpecTable` is a spec
run up to its zeroed end, from a Rust slice or scanned from C's pointer. The bit-fields go through
bindgen's `*_raw` accessors. `Kind`'s and `Status`'s `from_raw`/`raw` lost their `dead_code`
expectations, now that the accessors call them. Every accessor is anchored on its field, 23 in
all. `kind()` and `status()` return `None` for a value `opt.h` does not name. The allowlist gains
the three structs and `cli_opt_parse`, for the equivalence tests, on top of batch 1's
`cli_opt_parser_init` and `cli_opt_parser_next`. The bindings were regenerated after the rebase,
`+21` lines.

Tests: 17 `unit_pub` tests (every target round-tripped and retyped, shared variables, the strings,
aliases and usage, tables and positions, `Arg`, `ArgsSlot`, the outcome's and the parser's fields,
the two bits apart, reordering), 6 `ub_safe` tests through `Parser::new` (no arguments, reading
back what C stored through aliased handles, `FORCE_GNU`, reordering while variables, an outcome and
a slot keep what they took, a variable written through the table), 5 `equiv` tests, and 7
compile-fail doctests (lifetimes, invariance, `!Send`, the exclusive argument borrow). Four `equiv`
tests run C's `cli_opt_parser_next` and `cli_opt_parse` over tables built through the safe API.
After each step, every getter is compared with the fields as C laid them out, read from a copy of
the C struct, and each variable with what C stored. The setters' state is read by C: `in_literal`,
`idx`, `in_short` and `needs_sort`. The fifth reads values `opt.h` does not name as `None`. The CLI
has no C tests to carry over. Worklist coverage: `opt.rs` 538 of 539 lines, 114 of 114 functions,
565 of 566 regions. The one line is `ArgsSlot::get_in`'s refusal of a misaligned offset, which
neither safe code nor C can store. C `opt.c`: 71.22% of lines, 16 of 19 functions; the three left
are `cli_opt_foreach`, `cli_opt_status_fprint` and `spec_name_fprint`, the module's later symbols.

Coverage was measured with `crustify/scripts/coverage/run.sh` on the rebased tree and read with
`report.py` from the scratch tree's `src/` (`C=@c` over the `coverage` variant's `libcrustify.a`,
`Rust=.`), the unit column merging `lib` and `unit_pub`; the base is batch 1's measurement,
recorded in `Coverage stats`. The Rust shifts in suites that do not reach the new accessors are
their denominator's new lines. `equiv`'s `+0.20` pp C is the parser paths its tests reach. The
Overview's Rust LoC moves by ffimap's `code.loc.total` (`+533`, the regenerated bindings
included) and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+779`). `wrapped types` counts the three structs, and
`wrapped symbols` `cli_opt_parser_init`.

The safety audit scan (ffimap `9aa2ef1`, `--ffibox`, `--sys-crates pcre2_sys`, the 13 seams,
`--regions ffi_import,ffi_export`, no export feature) is compared with batch 1's scan of the tip.
The boundary scan's sites hold none in the changeset, and no public raw pointer or `unsafe fn` is
added. `&cell` `+1` is `SpecTable::new`'s `&[Spec]`, a borrow of a Rust-held array. `C by value`
`+9` is the three layouts holding their C structs, as `define_ctype!` does. The `raw→std` `+10`
and `raw deref` `+46` are the getters' strings, variables and argument slices, each tied to `'p`
or the handle's borrow. `ffimap api` against the tip, with ffibox's private rustdoc JSON (nightly
`2026-10-08`), finds all 30 keys `new`. `git2::src::cli::opt` is `new` among the unattributed
modules, for `Arg`, `ArgsSlot`, `SpecTable` and `Target`. `sys::git2` is `changed` only because
`cli_opt`, `cli_opt_parser` and `cli_opt_spec` are now tied to their layouts' anchors, and
`cli_opt_parse` is added.

Gates, all on the rebased tree (`29ec3ab87` plus this batch): the workspace is formatted, and
`clippy --all-targets` passes with warnings denied. The whole workspace passes on `plain` (`lib`
844 and 1 ignored, `ub_safe` 768, `ub_unsafe` 120, `equiv` 539, `unit_pub` 98, `hidden_symbols`
1, doctests 74 merged and 385 standalone). The module's tests (`lib` 4, `unit_pub` 31, `ub_safe`
6, `equiv` 11) pass under ASan+UBSan. Under Miri all pass but those that stop at the boundary:
this batch's nine are each run alone there and seen to stop at `cli_opt_parser_init` or
`cli_opt_parse` (`calls C`). The coverage run's nightly doctests checked the seven compile-fail
codes. The only failure there is the known `CommitBuilder` doctest. TSan has no obligation, with
no `Send` or `Sync` claim and no thread. BSan is no gate of this batch, and was not run. The raw
bindings changed, so the crate was packaged in bundled mode (698 files) and verified, by batch
0's command. Proposals: `type-erased-field-tagged-by-a-sibling` (`binding-types`, crustify
`755ff2c` on its evolution branch) and `compile-fail-doctest-codes-unchecked-on-stable`
(`testing`). Usage cells are the assistant's.

### `git2/src/cli/opt.c` wave 186 batch 3: review of batches 0 and 2

    pointer findings submitted to the ownership store. Four unit_priv,
    eleven unit_pub (carrying over test_utf8__char_length), three doctests
    and six equiv tests. Proposals: export-signature-check (porting-symbols,
    made as crustify dfd557c on its evolution branch, awaiting review) and

#[must_use]
pub fn valid_prefix_len(bytes: &[u8]) -> usize {
    let mut offset = 0;
    while let Some(len) = sequence_len(&bytes[offset..]) {
        offset += len;
    }
    offset
}

/// The gateway through which the C that remains calls this module once it has switched:
/// `git_utf8_iterate`, `git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length`, each
/// checked against its raw binding's signature, so that a C declaration that drifts fails
/// to build.
#[cfg(feature = "ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c")]
mod ffi_export {
    "/c/deps/ntlmclient/**",
    "/c/deps/reftable/**",
    "/c/deps/xdiff/**",
]

[features]
# Every link unit, so that the campaign's builds, lints and tests, which take the default

default = ["libgit2", "git2"]

libgit2 = []

bindgen = ["dep:bindgen"]
# Builds `c/` as shared libraries in place of static ones.
shared = []
# Links an install of libgit2, found through LIBGIT2_DIR or pkg-config, in place of `c/`.
system = []

# By path, not by Git: trybuild replaces only the paths of dependencies declared by path
# with `$FFIBOX` in compile-fail snapshots. By the checkout's canonical path, which
# /opt/venv/share/ffibox links to: trybuild replaces the canonicalized path, while rustc
# prints the path as declared, so a path through the link leaves the snapshots' paths

pcre2-sys = "0.2"
nix = { version = "0.31.3", features = ["fs", "socket", "net", "poll", "process", "user", "feature", "signal", "mman", "time", "uio", "dir", "hostname"] }
flate2 = "1.1.11"
sha2 = "0.11.1"
hmac = "0.13.0"
md-5 = "0.11.0"
md4 = "0.11.0"
des = "0.9.0"
getrandom = "0.4.3"
rustls = "0.23.46"
rustls-webpki = "0.103.16"
pcre2 = "0.2.11"

library.

## 2. Standard-library equivalents

The campaign's Rust reaches an out-of-tree library's entity through the Rust standard
library wherever the state the entity works on stays in Rust, or crosses to C only as
values the boundary converts, and through the library's wrapper wherever that state is
shared with C, as [`binding`](../../rust/binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section describes. The plan recommends which for each entity, from what it knows of the
uses; the batch that first needs the entity judges it from the code, as
[Confirmation](#8-confirmation) describes, so a wrapper covers what the campaign's Rust
reaches through it as its waves need it.

## 3. Side campaigns

A wrapper's work is a side campaign, continued in its own repository: it keeps its own
settings, plan, schedule, branches, builds and accounting there, and its batches land on
its own wave branches, as any wrap campaign's do. Its scope is what the parent campaign
reaches through the wrapper, not the whole library, and it grows as the parent's waves
need more of it. Its settings are the parent's, but for its `campaign`, which is `wrap`, its
`source`, the library at the release the target links, and its `scope`; a settings change
the parent applies is applied to its side campaigns too.

The side campaign advances at the parent's pace. Before a parent wave starts, the
entities its items need through each library's wrapper are judged from the items, the
libraries their modules' `depends_on.external` records name and the entities they use:
every entity of a library the standard library does not replace, and of the others those
whose state the items share with the remaining C, as
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) describes. What the
wrapper lacks of them, the side campaign plans and runs waves to wrap; once those are
promoted to its working branch, the parent's pin, its library's `crustify_campaign.pin`
in `dependencies.json`, moves to that commit, and the parent wave starts. A batch that needs
an entity through a wrapper that lacks it reports it rather than reaching it through raw
bindings, and runs again once the side campaign has wrapped it. The parent ships
only once each wrapper it pins has shipped the commit it pins, each with the user's
approval.

Each wrapper's crate bundles its own raw bindings, generated from the library's headers,
as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes. While its `c/` is the whole
library, the crate builds by default in system mode, linking the system's copy, as the
other crates of a dependent's build that wrap the same library do, so that a process holds
## 8. Confirmation

An entity's route is a recommendation made before any of its uses was translated. The first
batch that binds or ports one of its users checks the route against the code it translates,
by the uses the entity's `match` and note describe, and reports what it found in its final
message, which is recorded as the entity's `confirmation`. Each later batch takes
the confirmed route.

When the route does not hold, the batch reaches the entity through another route the
library's `decision` already allows, in this order: the standard library, where
[Standard-library equivalents](#2-standard-library-equivalents) allows it; another crate the
decision adopts for the library; the decision's `uncovered` route. A `crustify-campaign`
route that the library's crustify campaign does not yet cover is reported, and advanced as
[Side campaigns](#3-side-campaigns) describes, before the batch runs again. Where no route
the decision allows serves the entity, because the library leaves nothing `uncovered` or
only a crate the user has not adopted would, the batch reports it, and it is put
to the user, whose answer is recorded among the decision's `overrides`.

content.content:
---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

/opt/venv/bin/wavefront
usage: wavefront [-h] [--config PATH]
                 repo_root {extract-ql,schedule,query} ...

Semantic analysis, ownership findings, and deterministic scheduling for C.

positional arguments:
  repo_root             Full path to the repository root. Explicit — Wavefront
                        never walks the filesystem to find it.
  {extract-ql,schedule,query}
    extract-ql          Run the T1 (entities) + T2 (edges) .ql batches against
                        the CodeQL database below the config's state_dir and
                        write one CSV per query under its codeql/{t1,t2}/. The
                        database is NOT created here — build the project under
                        `codeql database create` yourself first. Everything
                        else derives from these tables on demand. Takes
                        minutes — run it only when the extraction is genuinely
                        stale.
    schedule            Order every unit of the config's closure and schedule
                        its `schedule_seeds` with what they depend on, one
                        wave per layer.
    query               Read-only oracle. With no subject, every entity,
                        grouped by kind. `functions`/`globals`/`macros`/`struc
                        ts`/`unions`/`enums`/`typedefs` enumerate one kind
                        (filtered, as a name list) or introspect one (--name)
                        as the whole record. `files` lists the closure /
                        external section file sets. `dag` does the graph walks
                        (closure / layer / scc).

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --config PATH         Explicit wavefront-config.json for extraction, query,
                        or schedule. Relative paths are resolved from
                        REPO_ROOT.

content.content:
# Wavefront

Wavefront analyzes a C codebase and schedules its units in dependency order
for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into
the dependency graph, and its schedules order units by them. You can also
record pointer-level ownership and lifecycle properties for each type and
symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

## Requirements

- Python 3.13 or newer
- The [CodeQL CLI](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries), on `PATH`

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crustify-rs/wavefront.git
cd wavefront
python -m pip install -e .
codeql pack install src/
```

## Usage

```text
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH COMMAND ...
```

`REPO_ROOT` is the root of the C repository. `--config` names its
`wavefront-config.json`; a relative path is resolved from `REPO_ROOT`.

### Configuration

```json
{
  "state_dir": ".wavefront",
  "closure": {
    "impl_files": {"included": ["src/"], "excluded": ["src/tests/"]},
    "api_headers": {"included": ["include/widget.h"]}
  },
  "modules": [
    {"name": "src/mem.c", "files": ["src/mem.c", "src/mem.h"]},
    {"name": "src/widget.c", "files": ["src/widget.c", "include/widget.h"]}
  ],
  "schedule_seeds": ["include/widget.h"],
  "t3_dir": "t3"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state_dir` | Directory for the CodeQL database and tables, ownership findings, and caches. |
| `closure` | The program Wavefront analyzes, for its graph, queries and usage counts: `impl_files`, the sources and private headers that implement it, and `api_headers`, the headers that publish its API, each `included` files and directories, less what `excluded` matches. See [Files](docs/scoping.md#files). |
| `modules` | Optional. Module records, `{name, files}`, each file entry as in `schedule_seeds`: a module is a named group of files and items, typically a TU with its headers, unrelated to C++20 modules. A schedule orders each module's units together, the modules in dependency order with their cycles cut. A unit no module claims is ordered alone. See [Modules](docs/scoping.md#modules). |
| `schedule_seeds` | Optional. What `wavefront schedule` starts from: a list of file entries, each seeding what its file defines or declares; a schedule holds its seeds and what they depend on. A file entry is a path, a directory written with a trailing slash, or `{path, items}` whose `included` and `excluded` items, each `{name, kind}`, narrow what it seeds. Without it, every unit of the closure. See [Schedule seeds](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds). |
| `t3_dir` | Optional. Directory, relative to `state_dir`, holding the T3 tables ([`examples/t3/`](examples/t3/)). |

Paths are relative to `REPO_ROOT`. A trailing slash selects a directory
recursively, in `included` and `excluded` alike; `excluded` is optional. See [`examples/wavefront-config.json`](examples/wavefront-config.json).

### 1. Extract

Build the project under CodeQL, then extract the T1 (entity) and T2 (edge)
tables into `<state_dir>/codeql/`:

```sh
codeql database create REPO_ROOT/.wavefront/codeql/db \
  --language=cpp --source-root=REPO_ROOT --command="make -j"
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config wavefront-config.json extract-ql
```

Run `extract-ql` again only when the database changes.

### 2. Query

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query [SUBJECT] [FLAGS]
```

| Subject | Output |
|---|---|
| none | Every entity, one `name`, `kind`, `defined_in`, `declared_in` line each, grouped by kind. `--closure-only`, `--external-only`, `--api-only` and `--file` narrow it. |
| `functions`, `globals`, `macros`, `function_pointers`, `typedefs` | Records of that kind: signatures, callers and callees, and findings. A function pointer is a typedef declaring one, its aliases folded in, or one written inline, named by its signature. A typedef is one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer. |
| `structs`, `unions`, `enums` | Records of that kind: fields, casts, users, and findings. |
| `files` | The closure, external, and API file sets. |
| `dag` | Dependency closures, graph layers, and cycle twins. |

Common flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Select entities by name. Without it, a kind's subject lists its names. |
| `--file FILE ...` | Narrow named entities to those defined in these files. |
| `--closure-only`, `--external-only` | Keep entities defined in the closure's files, or the external ones it reaches. |
| `--api-only` | Keep entities the `api_headers` publish. |
| `--update FINDINGS` | Submit findings for one named entity (`-` reads stdin). |
| `--in-tree`, `--out-of-tree` | Listing only: keep entities defined inside, or outside, the repository. |

Struct, union and enum views (one `--name`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--fields` | Print the declared fields and their records. |
| `--lifecycle-ops` | Print the routines that drop, dispose, clone, or construct the type. |
| `--users` | Print every function that uses the type, and for an enum every global and macro that names one of its constants. |
| `--field-touchers` | Print each field and the functions that access it. |
| `--layout-users` | Print every function, global and aggregate that depends on the type's layout, with the sites of each use. |
| `--raw-sites` | Print every function that allocates or frees the type with a raw routine (a lifecycle role on a `void *`, in the ownership store), with each site. With `--unresolved` and no `--name`: the raw sites on type-erased values no table types. |

Function searches (`--callees` and `--callers` also take a global, macro or typedef):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--taking SPEC` | Find functions with an argument of type `SPEC` (a type, `void`, or `string`). |
| `--returning SPEC` | Find functions that return a pointer of type `SPEC`. |
| `--lifetime-for SPEC` | Find the submitted lifecycle routines acting on `SPEC`. |
| `--calling FN,...` | With `--taking` or `--returning`, keep functions that reach one of `FN`. |
| `--callees`, `--callers` | Walk the call graph forward or backward from `--name`. |
| `--depth N` | Hop limit for the walks above; default `1`. |
| `--array` | Keep matches classified as arrays. |

Graph views (`query dag`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Print the dependency closure of the named nodes. |
| `--depth N` | Limit the closure to `N` hops. |
| `--layer N` | Print every node in layer `N`. |
| `--scc hi-deps\|lo-deps` | With `--name`, print the cycle twins recorded in `fallback` or `back_fill`. |
| `--loc` | Report estimated lines of code. |
| `--kind KIND` | With `--name`, keep its nodes of this kind (`function`, `struct`, ...). A name that names several nodes resolves to all of them, listed under `matches` with their kinds and files. |
| `--api-headers-only` | Use the public-signature graph. |

Examples:

```sh
# List everything the headers publish, by kind.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json query --api-only

# Show one type's fields.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query structs --name widget_st --fields

# Find functions that take widget_st and reach widget_release within 3 calls.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query functions --taking widget_st --calling widget_release --depth 3

# Show the dependencies of widget_new.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query dag --name widget_new --depth 1
```

Each subject's `--help` lists its complete flags.

A type or symbol record has two parts: `composed`, which Wavefront derives
from the code, and `findings`, which users fill. `findings` lists every slot
the entity accepts, in the shape `--update` takes, so a user can fill it in
and submit it. See [`docs/artifacts/findings.md`](docs/artifacts/findings.md)
and [`examples/findings.json`](examples/findings.json).

### 3. Schedule

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH schedule --output PATH [FLAGS]
```

A schedule orders every unit of the config's closure, in the groups its
[`modules`](docs/scoping.md#modules) make, keeps its
[`schedule_seeds`](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds) and every unit they depend
on, and emits one wave per layer of each module. A unit no module claims
goes in a wave of the first module that needs it, ahead of the wave that
does, or in a wave of its own when it is a seed, or what only such a seed
needs. A narrow schedule keeps the order and cuts of the whole
closure, so a consumer can schedule parts of a library in turn without
changing the order. Each unit carries its module, its `defined_in` and
`declared_in` files, and the statistics a consumer weighs its work by. A
struct, union or enum also carries the point after which none of its layout
users is left to process, `opaque_after`, and a struct or union the point
after which no C allocates or frees it with a raw routine,
`memory_unmanaged_after`; a function, global, macro, function pointer or
typedef the point after which none of its referrers is, `unreferenced_after`
([Release points](docs/batching.md#release-points)).

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| `--output PATH` | | Required. Output file; its directory must exist. |
| `--api-headers-only` | | Schedule the public API from the public-signature graph. |
| `--max-types N` | none | Types per type batch. |
| `--min-fields N` | none | Declared fields that close a type batch. |
| `--max-syms N` | none | Symbols per symbol batch. |
| `--max-loc N` | none | Body lines per symbol batch; `0` disables the limit. |

Without a cap, a wave holds two batches, its types and generator macros, then
everything else, for the consumer to split.

Example:

```sh
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json schedule \
  --api-headers-only --output /src/widget/schedule.json
```

See [`examples/schedule.json`](examples/schedule.json) for the output.

## Documentation

| Document | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`docs/graph.md`](docs/graph.md) | The dependency graph: nodes, edges, type erasure, cycles, polymorphism, and limitations. |
| [`docs/scoping.md`](docs/scoping.md) | The closure, modules, the schedule seeds, closure and external entities, the API view, and default and API modes. |
| [`docs/batching.md`](docs/batching.md) | Units, their order, waves, batch caps, and release points. |
| [`docs/pointer-properties.md`](docs/pointer-properties.md) | The pointer properties recorded in the ownership store. |
| [`docs/type-lifecycle.md`](docs/type-lifecycle.md) | Lifecycle roles, and how to find the routines that play them. |
| [`docs/artifacts/`](docs/artifacts/) | Field reference for type and symbol records, findings, the ownership store, schedules, and T3 tables. |

## Tests

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The default suite runs no CodeQL. A fixture's tests that compose, query or
schedule it read its committed tables, `tests/fixtures/<name>/codeql/`. The
tests that build each fixture's database and run the queries, checking the
queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

```sh
WAVEFRONT_CODEQL_TESTS=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

After such a change, re-extract the committed tables and review their diff:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python tests/regenerate_tables.py [FIXTURE ...]
```

## Maintainers

- Marius Momeu, marius.momeu@berkeley.edu

This material is based upon work supported by the Defense Advanced Research
Projects Agency (DARPA) Translating All C To Rust (TRACTOR) program under
Agreement No. HR00112590134.
# Pointer properties

A C pointer type states where a pointer points, but not how much it points
at, who releases it, or whether it may be null. A user records those facts
as a pointer's properties, in the ownership store
([`artifacts/ownership-store.md`](artifacts/ownership-store.md)). A Rust
translation reads them to choose the pointer's Rust type: a reference, a
slice, a string, an owning box, an `Option`.

## Where pointers occur

The same block of properties, `ptr`, describes a pointer wherever it occurs:

| site | record | ownership is relative to |
|---|---|---|
| parameter | `ptr_args[].ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the callee takes it, or borrows it |
| return | `ptr_ret.ptr` on a function or callback | the call: the caller receives it, or borrows it |
| field | `fields[].ptr` on a type | the enclosing struct |
| global | `ptr` on a global | the program |

A composed record carries `ptr: null` until a user submits a block, so
`null` means the pointer has not been analyzed. A submitted block replaces
the previous one entirely and must be complete.

## Shape

Three properties state what the pointer points at. A pointer sets at least
one of them, and may set several when different execution paths use it
differently.

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `scalar` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a single pointee: one value (`by_val`, an ordinary `T *`), or one pointer (`by_ref`, a `T **` such as an out-parameter). |
| `array` | `null`, `{by_val: true}`, or `{by_ref: {owned, borrowed}}` | On some path the pointer refers to a buffer: of values (`by_val`), or of pointers (`by_ref`, a container). |
| `string` | `true` or `false` | On some path the pointer refers to a NUL-terminated string. |

Under `by_ref`, `owned` and `borrowed` describe the inner pointers, the
pointee of a `T **` or the elements of a container, with the same
meaning as at the top level. The top-level `owned` and `borrowed` then
describe the outer pointer. `scalar.by_ref` and `array.by_ref` differ only
in how many inner pointers there are.

## Ownership

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `owned` | `true` or `false` | Whoever holds the pointer must release it. A parameter's ownership passes to the callee; a return's passes to the caller; a field's belongs to the struct. |
| `borrowed` | `null` or `{lifetime}` | The pointer is valid only while another entity is; `lifetime` names it. |

A pointer is owned, borrowed, or both; never neither. Both are set when
ownership depends on the path taken: owned on one, borrowed on another. The
same holds for each `by_ref` inner pointer.

A borrowed lifetime names its source in the vocabulary of the site:

| site | sources |
|---|---|
| parameter, return | `arg:<name>`, `arg:<name>-><path>`, `static`, `other` |
| field | `self` (the enclosing struct), `field:<name>` (a sibling field's storage), `static`, `other` |
| global | `static`, `other` |

A parameter is always named by its name, never by its position: in an
`arg:<name>` lifetime, and as the key of `ptr_args` in a submission. A
pointer that is read only during the call borrows from itself:
`arg:<its own name>`.

## Access

| property | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nullable` | `true` or `false` | The pointer may be `NULL`. |
| `mutable` | `true`, `false`, or `null` | Code writes through the pointer. A `const` pointee forces `false`; `null` only when it cannot be determined, as for an external function with no body. |
| `note` | text | The reasoning behind the block, and its gaps and corner cases. |

## Invariants

`query --update` rejects a block, and applies nothing, unless:

- `scalar` and `array` are each `null` or exactly one of `by_val` and
  `by_ref`;
- at least one of `scalar`, `array` and `string` is set;
- `string` and `owned` are booleans, never `null`;
- the pointer, and each `by_ref` inner pointer, is owned or borrowed;
- a borrowed pointer has a lifetime, and an `arg:<name>` lifetime names a
  parameter of the same symbol;
- a `const` pointee has `mutable` other than `true`;
- `ptr_ret` is set only on a symbol that returns a pointer.

## Related bindings

Two more judgements sit beside `ptr` on a field or a global, because they
apply to non-pointer data as well:

- `refcount` marks the one field that stores its type's reference count
  ([`type-lifecycle.md`](type-lifecycle.md));
- `locked_by` names the lock that guards a field or global, and the
  routines that acquire and release it: `{lock, lock_op, unlock_op}`.
# Findings schema

Field meaning for findings: the judgements a user records about an entity,
which wavefront cannot derive from the source. Every type and symbol record
that `query` prints has two parts:

```json
{"composed": {}, "findings": {}, "_analysis": {}}
```

`composed` is what wavefront derives from the CodeQL tables
([`types.md`](types.md), [`syms.md`](syms.md)). `findings` lists every slot a
user may fill for the entity, with `null` where nothing is recorded, in
exactly the shape `--update` accepts:

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query functions --name widget_new --update findings.json
```

A user can therefore copy a record's `findings`, fill it in, and submit it.
[`examples/findings.json`](../../examples/findings.json) holds a filled
example of each kind. `--update` validates the whole document against the
composed record and applies nothing if any rule fails; the error lists every
failure. Accepted findings are kept in the ownership store
([`ownership-store.md`](ownership-store.md)).

## Types

```json
{
  "_comment_user": "...",
  "fields": {
    "<field name>": {"ptr": {}, "refcount": false, "locked_by": null}
  }
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `_comment_user` | Free-text note on the type: the reasoning behind its findings. |
| `fields` | One entry per declared field, keyed by the field's name. |
| `fields.<name>.ptr` | The field's pointer properties ([`pointer-properties.md`](../pointer-properties.md)); pointer fields only. |
| `fields.<name>.refcount` | `true` on the one field that stores the type's reference count: the value an up-ref increments and a down-ref decrements ([`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)). |
| `fields.<name>.locked_by` | The lock that guards the field, pointer or not: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

A type has no lifecycle slot. Its lifecycle routines record their roles on
their own symbol records.

## Symbols

The slots depend on the symbol's kind.

**Functions and callbacks:**

```json
{
  "ptr_args": {"<arg name>": {"ptr": {}}},
  "ptr_ret": {"ptr": {}},
  "lifetime": null
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr_args` | One entry per pointer parameter, keyed by the parameter's name (never its position). |
| `ptr_args.<name>.ptr` | The parameter's pointer properties. |
| `ptr_ret.ptr` | The returned pointer's properties; present only when the symbol returns a pointer. |
| `lifetime` | The symbol's [lifecycle role](#lifetime), or `null`. |

**Callbacks** take `forks` as well: see [Forks](#forks).

**Globals:**

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ptr` | The global's pointer properties, when it stores a pointer; `null` otherwise. |
| `locked_by` | The lock that guards the global: `null`, or a [lock binding](#lock-binding). |

**Macros** take no findings.

A symbol has no note slot: the reasoning behind a pointer's properties goes
in that pointer's `ptr.note`.

### lifetime

The lifecycle role the symbol plays, and the object it acts on.

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `for` | The parameter the role acts on, by name (`s`, not `arg:s` or a position); or `"return"` for an `alloc` constructor that returns its object. |
| `is_dropper` | The symbol frees the object's own storage: a full destructor. |
| `is_disposer` | The symbol frees what the object's fields own, and keeps the object's storage: a cleanup or reset. |
| `is_cloner` | `null`, or `{deep, upref}`: the symbol copies the object. `deep` is a new, independent allocation; `upref` a reference-count increment that returns the same object. Both may be set when the copy depends on the path taken. |
| `is_constructor` | `null`, or `{alloc, init}`: the symbol produces an object. `alloc` hands the caller a new object it owns, returned or stored through a `T **` out-parameter; `init` initializes caller-provided storage in place. Exactly one is set. |

`--update` rejects a `lifetime` block unless:

- it sets at least one role; `null` states that the symbol has none;
- `for` names one of the symbol's pointer parameters, or is `"return"` on an
  `alloc` constructor that returns a pointer;
- an `alloc` through a parameter names a `T **` (depth 2 or more), and an
  `init` a `T *` (depth 1);
- `is_dropper` and `is_disposer` are not both set, and a constructor sets no
  other role;
- the mode flags of `is_cloner` and `is_constructor` are booleans, and
  `alloc` and `init` are not both set;
- the subject's pointer properties agree: a dropper's argument is owned, a
  cloner's is borrowed, an `alloc` constructor's return is owned, and a
  constructor's argument is not immutable.

The last rule reads the subject's `ptr` as it stands after the update, and is
skipped while that `ptr` is `null`. [`type-lifecycle.md`](../type-lifecycle.md)
describes the roles and how to find the routines that play them.

### Forks

A callback whose invokers realize different contracts is split into forks:
one record per contract, each with its own pointer properties and role. On
the callback's primary record, `forks` lists them:

```json
{
  "forks": [
    {"ptr_args": {}, "ptr_ret": {}, "lifetime": null, "callsites": ["<invoker>"]}
  ]
}
```

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `forks[].ptr_args`, `ptr_ret`, `lifetime` | The fork's own findings, as on the primary. |
| `forks[].callsites` | The invokers that realize this fork's contract; the primary keeps the rest. Each invoker belongs to at most one fork. |

Each fork's own record shows its findings with its `callsites`. Forks are
submitted through the primary's `forks`, which replaces every earlier fork.

## Lock binding

`locked_by` names the lock that guards a field or a global:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `lock` | The field or global that stores the lock object. |
| `lock_op` | The routines that acquire it. Which ones appear shows how readers and writers lock. |
| `unlock_op` | The routines that release it. |

## Merging

`--update` merges a submission into what is already recorded:

- a type's fields merge one by one, and each named key replaces its value;
  `_comment_user` is replaced when present;
- a symbol's parameters merge one by one, and a `ptr` block replaces the
  previous one entirely, so it must be complete;
- a `null` slot clears what was recorded: a field's or a parameter's `ptr`,
  the return's `ptr`, a global's `ptr`, `lifetime`, and `locked_by`;
- a slot the submission omits is left as it is;
- `forks` replaces every earlier fork of the callback.

Submitting a record's own `findings` unchanged therefore leaves every
recorded value as it is, and `null` is how a wrong finding is withdrawn.

# Wavefront

for translation to Rust. It extracts entities and dependencies with CodeQL,
builds a cycle-free dependency graph of the codebase's types and symbols, and
packs that graph into ordered waves of batches. Each batch can be translated
once the waves before it are complete.

Wavefront keeps its analysis simple: it infers facts from the codebase without
data-flow or points-to analysis. It is built for neuro-symbolic workflows, in
which human or LLM reasoning complements its static facts. You can state the
polymorphic and type-erased edges it cannot infer; Wavefront loads them into
the dependency graph, and its schedules order units by them. You can also
record pointer-level ownership and lifecycle properties for each type and
symbol, which Wavefront returns with their records.

## Requirements

- Python 3.13 or newer
- The [CodeQL CLI](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries), on `PATH`

## Installation

```sh
git clone https://github.com/crustify-rs/wavefront.git
cd wavefront
python -m pip install -e .
codeql pack install src/
```

## Usage

```text
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH COMMAND ...
```

`REPO_ROOT` is the root of the C repository. `--config` names its
`wavefront-config.json`; a relative path is resolved from `REPO_ROOT`.

### Configuration

```json
{
  "state_dir": ".wavefront",
  "closure": {
    "impl_files": {"included": ["src/"], "excluded": ["src/tests/"]},
    "api_headers": {"included": ["include/widget.h"]}
  },
  "modules": [
    {"name": "src/mem.c", "files": ["src/mem.c", "src/mem.h"]},
    {"name": "src/widget.c", "files": ["src/widget.c", "include/widget.h"]}
  ],
  "schedule_seeds": ["include/widget.h"],
  "t3_dir": "t3"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state_dir` | Directory for the CodeQL database and tables, ownership findings, and caches. |
| `closure` | The program Wavefront analyzes, for its graph, queries and usage counts: `impl_files`, the sources and private headers that implement it, and `api_headers`, the headers that publish its API, each `included` files and directories, less what `excluded` matches. See [Files](docs/scoping.md#files). |
| `modules` | Optional. Module records, `{name, files}`, each file entry as in `schedule_seeds`: a module is a named group of files and items, typically a TU with its headers, unrelated to C++20 modules. A schedule orders each module's units together, the modules in dependency order with their cycles cut. A unit no module claims is ordered alone. See [Modules](docs/scoping.md#modules). |
| `schedule_seeds` | Optional. What `wavefront schedule` starts from: a list of file entries, each seeding what its file defines or declares; a schedule holds its seeds and what they depend on. A file entry is a path, a directory written with a trailing slash, or `{path, items}` whose `included` and `excluded` items, each `{name, kind}`, narrow what it seeds. Without it, every unit of the closure. See [Schedule seeds](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds). |
| `t3_dir` | Optional. Directory, relative to `state_dir`, holding the T3 tables ([`examples/t3/`](examples/t3/)). |

Paths are relative to `REPO_ROOT`. A trailing slash selects a directory
recursively, in `included` and `excluded` alike; `excluded` is optional. See [`examples/wavefront-config.json`](examples/wavefront-config.json).

### 1. Extract

Build the project under CodeQL, then extract the T1 (entity) and T2 (edge)
tables into `<state_dir>/codeql/`:

```sh
codeql database create REPO_ROOT/.wavefront/codeql/db \
  --language=cpp --source-root=REPO_ROOT --command="make -j"
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config wavefront-config.json extract-ql
```

Run `extract-ql` again only when the database changes.

### 2. Query

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH query [SUBJECT] [FLAGS]
```

| Subject | Output |
|---|---|
| none | Every entity, one `name`, `kind`, `defined_in`, `declared_in` line each, grouped by kind. `--closure-only`, `--external-only`, `--api-only` and `--file` narrow it. |
| `functions`, `globals`, `macros`, `function_pointers`, `typedefs` | Records of that kind: signatures, callers and callees, and findings. A function pointer is a typedef declaring one, its aliases folded in, or one written inline, named by its signature. A typedef is one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer. |
| `structs`, `unions`, `enums` | Records of that kind: fields, casts, users, and findings. |
| `files` | The closure, external, and API file sets. |
| `dag` | Dependency closures, graph layers, and cycle twins. |

Common flags:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Select entities by name. Without it, a kind's subject lists its names. |
| `--file FILE ...` | Narrow named entities to those defined in these files. |
| `--closure-only`, `--external-only` | Keep entities defined in the closure's files, or the external ones it reaches. |
| `--api-only` | Keep entities the `api_headers` publish. |
| `--update FINDINGS` | Submit findings for one named entity (`-` reads stdin). |
| `--in-tree`, `--out-of-tree` | Listing only: keep entities defined inside, or outside, the repository. |

Struct, union and enum views (one `--name`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--fields` | Print the declared fields and their records. |
| `--lifecycle-ops` | Print the routines that drop, dispose, clone, or construct the type. |
| `--users` | Print every function that uses the type, and for an enum every global and macro that names one of its constants. |
| `--field-touchers` | Print each field and the functions that access it. |
| `--layout-users` | Print every function, global and aggregate that depends on the type's layout, with the sites of each use. |
| `--raw-sites` | Print every function that allocates or frees the type with a raw routine (a lifecycle role on a `void *`, in the ownership store), with each site. With `--unresolved` and no `--name`: the raw sites on type-erased values no table types. |

Function searches (`--callees` and `--callers` also take a global, macro or typedef):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--taking SPEC` | Find functions with an argument of type `SPEC` (a type, `void`, or `string`). |
| `--returning SPEC` | Find functions that return a pointer of type `SPEC`. |
| `--lifetime-for SPEC` | Find the submitted lifecycle routines acting on `SPEC`. |
| `--calling FN,...` | With `--taking` or `--returning`, keep functions that reach one of `FN`. |
| `--callees`, `--callers` | Walk the call graph forward or backward from `--name`. |
| `--depth N` | Hop limit for the walks above; default `1`. |
| `--array` | Keep matches classified as arrays. |

Graph views (`query dag`):

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--name NAME ...` | Print the dependency closure of the named nodes. |
| `--depth N` | Limit the closure to `N` hops. |
| `--layer N` | Print every node in layer `N`. |
| `--scc hi-deps\|lo-deps` | With `--name`, print the cycle twins recorded in `fallback` or `back_fill`. |
| `--loc` | Report estimated lines of code. |
| `--kind KIND` | With `--name`, keep its nodes of this kind (`function`, `struct`, ...). A name that names several nodes resolves to all of them, listed under `matches` with their kinds and files. |
| `--api-headers-only` | Use the public-signature graph. |

Examples:

```sh
# List everything the headers publish, by kind.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json query --api-only

# Show one type's fields.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query structs --name widget_st --fields

# Find functions that take widget_st and reach widget_release within 3 calls.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query functions --taking widget_st --calling widget_release --depth 3

# Show the dependencies of widget_new.
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json \
  query dag --name widget_new --depth 1
```

Each subject's `--help` lists its complete flags.

A type or symbol record has two parts: `composed`, which Wavefront derives
from the code, and `findings`, which users fill. `findings` lists every slot
the entity accepts, in the shape `--update` takes, so a user can fill it in
and submit it. See [`docs/artifacts/findings.md`](docs/artifacts/findings.md)
and [`examples/findings.json`](examples/findings.json).

### 3. Schedule

```sh
wavefront REPO_ROOT --config PATH schedule --output PATH [FLAGS]
```

A schedule orders every unit of the config's closure, in the groups its
[`modules`](docs/scoping.md#modules) make, keeps its
[`schedule_seeds`](docs/scoping.md#schedule-seeds) and every unit they depend
on, and emits one wave per layer of each module. A unit no module claims
goes in a wave of the first module that needs it, ahead of the wave that
does, or in a wave of its own when it is a seed, or what only such a seed
needs. A narrow schedule keeps the order and cuts of the whole
closure, so a consumer can schedule parts of a library in turn without
changing the order. Each unit carries its module, its `defined_in` and
`declared_in` files, and the statistics a consumer weighs its work by. A
struct, union or enum also carries the point after which none of its layout
users is left to process, `opaque_after`, and a struct or union the point
after which no C allocates or frees it with a raw routine,
`memory_unmanaged_after`; a function, global, macro, function pointer or
typedef the point after which none of its referrers is, `unreferenced_after`
([Release points](docs/batching.md#release-points)).

| Flag | Default | Effect |
|---|---:|---|
| `--output PATH` | | Required. Output file; its directory must exist. |
| `--api-headers-only` | | Schedule the public API from the public-signature graph. |
| `--max-types N` | none | Types per type batch. |
| `--min-fields N` | none | Declared fields that close a type batch. |
| `--max-syms N` | none | Symbols per symbol batch. |
| `--max-loc N` | none | Body lines per symbol batch; `0` disables the limit. |

Without a cap, a wave holds two batches, its types and generator macros, then
everything else, for the consumer to split.

Example:

```sh
wavefront /src/widget --config wavefront-config.json schedule \
  --api-headers-only --output /src/widget/schedule.json
```

See [`examples/schedule.json`](examples/schedule.json) for the output.

## Tests

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

The default suite runs no CodeQL. A fixture's tests that compose, query or
schedule it read its committed tables, `tests/fixtures/<name>/codeql/`. The
tests that build each fixture's database and run the queries, checking the
queries' golden tables and that the committed tables are current, are
opt-in, and pass before a change to a query or a fixture's C lands:

```sh
WAVEFRONT_CODEQL_TESTS=1 PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

After such a change, re-extract the committed tables and review their diff:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=src python tests/regenerate_tables.py [FIXTURE ...]
```
